title: Part 5
display: Part 5 — Selecting Hosts with Host Patterns; Managing Dynamic Invent…

content.text: hosts: in a play isn't limited to one group name — it accepts a genuine pattern language for precisely selecting who a play targets.
Any inventory name starting with datacenter

⚠ WARNING Wildcards match against ALL inventory names — hostnames, IP addresses, AND group names alike, with no way to distinguish between them. A pattern like data* could unexpectedly also match a group literally named data, not just hosts named data.example.com — always check what actually resolves with --list-hosts before trusting a wildcard pattern in production.
A comma-separated list matches any host that matches ANY item in the list — hosts, groups, and even wildcards can all be mixed together in one list.

🔎 REAL-WORLD EXTENSION A colon (:) works as the same separator in older playbooks, but the comma is now preferred — especially since a colon is ambiguous with IPv6 addresses used as host names. Recognize the colon syntax in older examples.
Logical AND with &, logical NOT with !
Hosts in the lab group AND in the datacenter1 group
All hosts in datacenter EXCEPT test2.example.com
Every host in the inventory EXCEPT those in datacenter1

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT The & (AND / intersection) and ! (NOT / exclusion) prefixes on list items are directly exam-relevant and easy to blank on under pressure. Memorize by name: comma alone is OR, & prefix is AND, ! prefix is NOT.

⚠ WARNING Special host-pattern characters (*, !, &) also mean something to the shell. Always wrap a host pattern containing them in single quotes on the ansible/ansible-playbook command line, and in a playbook's hosts: line, to stop the shell (or YAML) from misinterpreting them before Ansible ever sees the pattern.

A static inventory file is fine for a small, stable set of hosts. It breaks down in environments where machines come and go quickly — cloud auto-scaling groups, virtualization clusters, hosts tracked by an external CMDB. A dynamic inventory script queries that external source LIVE, every time Ansible runs, instead of relying on a hand-maintained text file that's always slightly out of date.
Red Hat Satellite, Cobbler, Foreman, Spacewalk
AWS EC2, OpenStack, Google Compute Engine

Community-contributed scripts for most of these already exist (from the Ansible GitHub project, unofficial/unsupported by Red Hat). If nothing exists for a given environment, a custom script can be written in ANY language, as long as it outputs valid JSON when called with --list.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT How Ansible decides static vs. dynamic: if the inventory FILE IS EXECUTABLE, Ansible treats it as a dynamic inventory script and runs it. If it's not executable, Ansible treats it as a plain static inventory file. This is purely a file-permission check — nothing about the file's name or content decides it.

ansible-inventory works against BOTH static and dynamic inventories, converting either into the same JSON structure — genuinely useful both for debugging a custom dynamic inventory script and for understanding exactly what Ansible sees before writing one yourself.

An inventory location can be a DIRECTORY containing several files (some static, some dynamic scripts) — Ansible merges them all into one combined inventory, parsed in alphabetical order. If a static file references a group that's actually populated by a dynamic source, that static file still needs a placeholder entry for the group name, so the merge stays internally consistent regardless of parse order:

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Assuming inventory files in a directory are parsed in the order that makes logical sense. They're parsed alphabetically by filename, regardless of dependencies between them — a naming convention (00-static, 10-dynamic-aws, etc.) is the practical fix when order genuinely matters.

Ansible doesn't connect to every managed host simultaneously by default — the forks setting (in ansible.cfg, default 5) caps how many connections run at once. With 10 hosts and forks=5, Ansible runs the first task on 5 hosts, then the same task on the remaining 5, THEN moves to the second task the same way.
[student@demo ~]$ ansible-playbook -f 20 site.yml # override for one run

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS forks=5 is deliberately conservative. If a control node is only managing Linux hosts (most modules run ON the managed host, not the control node), raising forks toward 100 is often a real, safe performance win. But if you're managing network devices where modules run ON the control node itself, the control node's own CPU/memory becomes the bottleneck — raise forks much more cautiously there.

Even with forks tuned high, Ansible by default still waits for EVERY host to finish a task before ANY host moves to the next task — which, for something like a web server restart, could take every server in a load-balanced pool offline at the same instant. serial: makes Ansible run hosts through the WHOLE PLAY in small batches instead.
- name: latest apache httpd package is installed

With five web servers and serial: 2, Ansible runs the ENTIRE play (every task, then any notified handlers) on the first 2 hosts, then repeats on the next 2, then the last 1 — so at most 2 servers are ever out of service simultaneously, and the majority stay available throughout.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Each serial batch is treated as if it were its OWN complete play. If an entire batch fails, the whole playbook run aborts immediately — the remaining, not-yet-processed hosts are simply never touched. This is intentional: it stops a bad rollout after a small, known-bad batch instead of pushing a broken change to every host.
serial: can also be given as a percentage of the total host count instead of a fixed number — the batch size is always at least 1 host, regardless of how small the percentage rounds down to.

A playbook that's grown into hundreds of lines is hard to review, hard to reuse pieces of, and hard to hand off to a teammate. Ansible has two distinct mechanisms for splitting content into separate files — import and include — and they behave meaningfully differently, not just stylistically.
STATIC — resolved when the playbook is first PARSED, before the run starts
Content is copy-pasted in ahead of time
DYNAMIC — resolved at RUN TIME, only when that point in the play is actually reached
Content is fetched and run on the fly

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT This static-vs-dynamic distinction is one of the highest-value facts in this entire chapter, because it explains a whole list of behavioral differences the exam tests individually. Learn the ONE underlying reason (when is it resolved?) rather than memorizing each symptom separately.

import_playbook only works at the TOP LEVEL of a playbook (never inside a play), and imported playbooks run in the order listed — they can even be interleaved with normal plays defined directly in the master file.
Both pull a flat list of tasks from a separate file into a play:
Applied to EACH task inside individually
Determines whether the WHOLE FILE is pulled in at all
Lists the INDIVIDUAL tasks from inside the file
Lists only the include_tasks line itself, not what's inside
CAN start mid-way inside the imported file
CANNOT start inside an included file
notify targeting a handler inside the file
N/A the same way — tasks are inserted directly
CANNOT target a handler defined inside the included file directly
Cannot use a host/group inventory variable for the filename
Works, since it's resolved at actual run time

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Trying to use loop: on an import_tasks call. It silently doesn't work the way you'd expect, because import_tasks is resolved before the play even starts running — there's no 'current item' concept yet at that point. Use include_tasks whenever a task file genuinely needs to be looped.
A task file becomes genuinely reusable once its specifics are turned into variables instead of hardcoded values:
- name: Import task file and set variables
The same vars: pattern works on import_playbook too — a single reusable play/task file can be called multiple times with different variable values instead of copy-pasting near-identical files.

🔎 REAL-WORLD EXTENSION Older Ansible material sometimes uses a single unified include directive for both playbooks and tasks, which behaved inconsistently across versions and is now deprecated in favor of the explicit import_*/include_* pairs covered here — recognize include in old documentation, but use the modern explicit forms.
View any inventory (static or dynamic) as JSON
Run the whole play in host batches (rolling update)
Statically insert a task list at parse time
Dynamically insert a task list at run time

labs.title: Lab: Precise Targeting + a Modular, Safe Rollout

content.text: Use host pattern logic to target an exact subset of hosts, split a playbook into reusable task files, and perform a safe rolling update with serial.

Your inventory has a webservers group (5 hosts) and a canary group that overlaps with ONE of those web servers, used for testing changes early. You need to: (1) run a quick check against every webserver except the canary, (2) roll out a package update across all five web servers two at a time, and (3) move the actual installation steps into a separate, reusable task file.
An inventory with [webservers] (5 hosts) and [canary] (1 host, also a member of webservers)
1. Write an ad hoc-style play targeting webservers,!canary-hostname (adjust to your actual canary hostname) that just pings
2. Create tasks/webapp_install.yml as a parameterized task file (package and service as variables) installing and starting a service
3. Write a rollout playbook that imports that task file with vars: set, targets webservers, and uses serial: 2 so no more than 2 servers update at once
4. Add a notify to restart the service, with a matching handler in the main playbook

The task file needs to use import_tasks (not include_tasks) here specifically so a when placed on the import (if you add one later) would apply per-task — but note import_tasks can't be looped, which is fine since this task file isn't looping.
Before checking the solution: run ansible webservers,!canary-hostname --list-hosts first to CONFIRM the pattern resolves to exactly 4 hosts (5 minus the canary) before trusting it in a real play.
- name: Ensure {{ service }} is enabled and started
'webservers,!canary1.lab.example.com' is a plain comma-list with a ! exclusion — matches every host in webservers EXCEPT the named canary.
serial: 2 on the rollout play means at most 2 of the 5 web servers are mid-update (and thus possibly briefly unavailable) at any moment — the other 3+ stay in service.
import_tasks pulls the parameterized file in at parse time, with vars: supplying package/service values so the same task file could be reused for a completely different piece of software elsewhere.

The handler lives in the IMPORTING playbook, not the task file — notify from inside an imported task file correctly reaches a handler defined in the main playbook, since import_tasks flattens everything into one play at parse time.

Watch the rollout playbook's output: hosts should be processed in visibly separate batches of 2 (then the final batch of 1), each batch completing its tasks AND any notified handler before the next batch begins — not all five hosts interleaved together.

This lab's shape — a canary-excluded sanity check, then a serial-batched rollout using a shared, parameterized task file — is genuinely how careful teams roll out changes to production web fleets: verify first, roll out gradually, keep the majority of capacity online throughout.
Q1. What host pattern targets every host in group A that is ALSO in group B?
Answer: A,&B — the & prefix means logical AND / intersection.
Q2. What host pattern targets every host in the inventory EXCEPT those in group X?
Answer: all,!X — the ! prefix means logical NOT / exclusion.
Q3. How does Ansible decide whether an inventory source is treated as static or dynamic?
Answer: Purely by whether the inventory FILE IS EXECUTABLE — executable means it's run as a dynamic inventory script; non-executable means it's parsed as a static file.
Q4. What command converts any inventory (static or dynamic) into a JSON view for inspection?
Q5. What does the forks setting control, and what's its default value?
Answer: The maximum number of simultaneous connections Ansible opens to managed hosts per task; the default is 5.
Q6. With serial: 2 across 5 hosts, if the FIRST batch of 2 fails, what happens to the remaining 3 hosts?
Answer: The entire playbook run aborts immediately — the remaining hosts are never processed, because each serial batch is treated as its own complete play.
Q7. What is the single underlying difference between import_* and include_*?
Answer: import_* is STATIC — resolved when the playbook is parsed, before the run starts; include_* is DYNAMIC — resolved at actual run time, when that point in the play is reached.
Q8. Can you use loop: on an import_tasks call?
Answer: No — import_tasks is resolved at parse time, before any 'current item' concept exists; use include_tasks if the task file needs to be looped.
Q9. Where must import_playbook be used — can it appear inside a play?
Answer: Only at the TOP LEVEL of a playbook — never inside a play, since it imports complete plays, not individual tasks.
Q10. How do you make an imported/included task file genuinely reusable across different contexts?
Answer: Parameterize the hardcoded values as Jinja2 variables inside the task file, then supply different values via vars: on each import_tasks/include_tasks (or import_playbook) call.
RH294 — RED HAT SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION III: LINUX AUTOMATION

This Part covers RH294 Chapter 8 in full: what a role is and how it's structured, reusing Red Hat's own pre-built RHEL System Roles, creating your own roles from scratch, and finding/installing community roles with Ansible Galaxy.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS Everything from Part 2 onward (variables, task control, templates, project structure) was really building toward this. A role packages all of it — tasks, handlers, variables, templates, files — into one reusable, shareable, drop-in unit. This is the single most production-relevant chapter in RH294: real Ansible codebases are organized almost entirely around roles, not flat playbooks.
